Earlier experiments already compared RNA encoders (PCA was best; scVI and scGPT were worse) and fusion (concat beat weighted). Transformer aggregation strongly beat avgpool in the RNA-only pair. The image encoder, however, has never been varied. Every image-based run used ViT-L, and ResNet50 is completely unexplored even though it appears in many remaining configurations. 2. What this tests: config_025 keeps everything from config_022 and swaps only the image encoder to ResNet50. This cleanly isolates how much of the multimodal gain depends on the image representation. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: the result either confirms ViT-L, letting us prune many ResNet50 configurations, or reveals a stronger image backbone to exploit. That reduces uncertainty about an untested design choice more than retesting dimensions we already have some evidence on.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_022 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. It clearly beats both unimodal transformer baselines (RNA 0.520, image 0.537). Within that setup, swapping the RNA encoder, the image encoder or the fusion method each hurt performance. The open question is the profile setting. For RNA-only, single-profile (0.512) and multiprofile with transformer (0.520) were nearly tied, so it is unclear whether multiprofile with transformer aggregation adds real value in the multimodal model. 2) Test: config_021 keeps everything from config_022 except the profile setting, which becomes single-profile. This isolates the effect of multiprofile with transformer aggregation in the best-performing pipeline. 3) Why now: this one-variable comparison resolves a key design uncertainty, and the result is useful either way. If single-profile matches or beats 0.619, the simpler pipeline is preferable. If it falls short, it confirms that multiprofile aggregation matters in the multimodal setting. Avgpool variants are a weaker choice for this slot, since avgpool already performed poorly for RNA-only.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so I know nothing yet about modality, representation, profile setting, aggregation or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_025 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA n2000, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest, most interpretable configuration in the space. It sets the reference accuracy and F1 that every later design choice can be measured against. It also has direct one-factor neighbours: scVI or scGPT encoders (config_015, config_039), multiprofile avgpool or transformer aggregation (config_013, config_026), and adding image features through multimodal fusion (config_005, config_049). 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, starting with a cheap baseline lets each later experiment change one design choice and isolate its effect. Starting with a complex multimodal multiprofile model would mix many factors together and make its result hard to attribute. This choice does not assume complexity helps, and it guards against overcrediting multimodal or multiprofile models later.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. The single-profile RNA baseline with PCA (n=2000) reached 0.471 accuracy and 0.442 F1. We do not yet know whether any other design dimension helps. 2. What this tests: config_013 keeps the same model setting (RNA only) and the same encoder (PCA n=2000). It changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (average pooling). This isolates whether multiprofile input adds value over the single-profile baseline. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: profile setting affects most of the remaining configurations, so learning its effect early narrows the search efficiently. Average pooling gives a clean first test before trying the more complex transformer aggregation. Modality comparisons (image-only and multimodal) can follow once we know which profile setting to anchor on.

1. Evidence: with the RNA-only PCA encoder, single-profile reached 0.471 accuracy and 0.442 F1. The multiprofile version with avgpool fell sharply to 0.227 accuracy and 0.191 F1. It is unclear whether multiprofile itself hurts or whether simple mean pooling is erasing useful profile-level signal. 2. Test: config_026 keeps everything from config_013 the same (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. If it recovers toward or beyond single-profile performance, aggregation was the bottleneck. If it stays low, multiprofile is likely harmful in this setting. 3. Why now: most untested configurations are multiprofile, so this single-variable comparison decides whether that large region deserves more budget. It is more informative than testing an image-only or multimodal option before this key design choice is understood.

1) Evidence so far: all three experiments are RNA-only with the PCA encoder. Multiprofile with transformer aggregation scored best (0.514 accuracy, 0.498 F1). Single-profile came next (0.471). Multiprofile with avgpool collapsed (0.227), so aggregation choice matters a great deal. The image modality is completely untested, which makes it the largest open question about whether multimodal configurations are worth exploring. 2) This experiment runs image-only with the ImageNet ViT-L encoder, using the multiprofile transformer setting that has worked best so far. It tells us how much signal images carry on their own, under an aggregation known to work, without adding fusion choices that would confound the result. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: if images are weak, we can focus the remaining budget on RNA encoders such as scVI and scGPT. If images are competitive, multimodal transformer configurations (e.g., config_046 or config_033) become well-motivated next steps. The comparison also adds evidence on whether the transformer's advantage carries over to another modality.

Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool for multiprofile RNA (0.514 vs 0.227 with pca_n2000), and multiprofile beats singleprofile for RNA with a transformer (0.514 vs 0.471). The best result so far is image-only ViT-L multiprofile with a transformer (0.537). Both unimodal transformer models perform reasonably, but it is unknown whether combining them helps. This experiment adds the tested pca_n2000 RNA branch to the best image setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) using simple concat fusion. Because it differs from the two unimodal configs only by adding the other modality, it directly tests whether multimodal fusion improves on either modality alone. It exploits the strongest direction found so far while answering the key open question about fusion. If it helps, weighted fusion (config_046) is the natural follow-up. If it does not, budget can shift to image encoder or RNA encoder comparisons.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is image-only ViT-L with multiprofile transformer aggregation (0.537 acc / 0.518 F1). Adding PCA RNA through concat fusion (config_033) dropped performance to 0.485 / 0.464, below image-only and close to the RNA-only transformer (0.514). Transformer aggregation is clearly better than avgpool, at least for RNA (0.514 vs 0.227). It is still unclear whether multimodality itself hurts or whether naive concat fusion lets the weaker RNA signal dilute the image features. 2. Test: config_046 changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, and keeps the same encoders, profile setting and aggregation as config_033. It cleanly isolates the fusion effect. If weighted fusion recovers or beats image-only performance, the multimodal deficit came from fusion. If it stays low, RNA integration is the problem, and later budget should go to RNA encoders or image-only refinements. 3. Why now: fusion is a key untested design choice that bears on every remaining multimodal configuration, which make up most of the search space. A single-variable comparison answers it efficiently, and the run also has a real chance of yielding a new best model.

Evidence: In the RNA-only multiprofile runs, transformer aggregation scored 0.514 accuracy and avgpool scored 0.227, so transformer aggregation looks strongly preferred. Image-only ViT-L with a transformer is the current best at 0.537 accuracy and 0.518 F1. Both multimodal runs paired ViT-L with PCA RNA features and did worse than image-only (concat 0.485, weighted 0.328). A likely explanation is a weak RNA representation, but every RNA result so far uses pca_n2000, so the effect of the RNA encoder is the largest unresolved uncertainty. Test: config_003 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA to scGPT, inside the best-known RNA setup (multiprofile, transformer). Its result can be compared directly with config_026. Why now: if scGPT improves clearly on PCA, it points to a better RNA branch for later multimodal fusion experiments. If it does not, that strengthens the case for focusing on image-only models or tuning fusion. Either way, the single-factor change answers a key question more cheaply than another multimodal run that changes several things at once.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is image_only, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l with transformer aggregation (0.537 acc, 0.518 F1). It beats the best RNA-only model (pca_n2000 + transformer, 0.514) and both multimodal fusions (concat 0.485, weighted 0.328). Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool for RNA (0.514 vs 0.227). Among RNA encoders, pca_n2000 beat scgpt (0.514 vs 0.332). The image encoder choice is still untested, although resnet50 appears in many remaining configurations. 2. Test: Running image_only, multiprofile, resnet50 with transformer aggregation changes only the image encoder relative to the current best. This isolates whether ViT-L matters or whether a different backbone could do better. 3. Why now: Image-only is the strongest modality so far, so its encoder is a high-value open question. The result will decide whether the many resnet50 multimodal options are worth pursuing, and it may also beat the current best. Testing scvi or other multimodal variants now would change more factors or address less promising directions.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation over multiple profiles is clearly the strongest setting so far. Image-only models reached about 0.54 accuracy with both ResNet50 and ViT-L, and RNA-only with PCA reached 0.514. Avgpool collapsed to 0.227. Adding RNA did not beat image-only: concat fusion gave 0.485 and weighted fusion 0.328. The RNA representation looks like the key bottleneck, since scGPT (0.332) was far worse than PCA (0.514) under the same setup. scVI is the one RNA encoder that has never been tested, yet it appears in many of the remaining multimodal configurations. 2) Test: run scVI as an RNA-only model with multiple profiles and transformer aggregation. This is a direct one-variable comparison against config_026 (PCA) and config_003 (scGPT), so it isolates the effect of RNA representation. 3) Why now: it resolves the largest remaining uncertainty in the design space. If scVI beats PCA, it becomes the obvious RNA branch to pair with ResNet50 or ViT-L in later multimodal runs. If it does not, PCA is confirmed and many scVI multimodal configurations can be ruled out without spending budget on them.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool. PCA RNA went from 0.227 to 0.514 when avgpool was replaced. Image-only transformer models are the best so far, at about 0.54 for both ResNet50 and ViT-L. Among RNA encoders, scVI (0.520) is slightly ahead of PCA (0.514), and both are far ahead of scGPT (0.332). Multimodal fusion has underperformed: PCA+ViT concat scored 0.485, below image-only, and weighted fusion scored 0.328. Concat therefore looks like the better fusion choice. The open question is why multimodal underperforms. One possibility is the high-dimensional 2000-component PCA RNA input, which may dominate or add noise in concatenation. 2) Test: config_037 keeps everything from config_033 the same (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to the compact 200-dimensional scVI. This shows whether the multimodal deficit depends on the RNA representation. 3) Why now: this is a one-variable comparison on the main unresolved question, whether fusion can beat unimodal models. It also exploits the strongest settings found so far (transformer aggregation, concat fusion, the best RNA encoder). Swapping the image encoder instead would teach less, because ResNet50 and ViT-L performed almost identically on their own.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2. What this tests: an RNA-only, single-profile model with the compact scVI (n200) encoder. It is the simplest configuration and has no aggregation or fusion choices, so it gives a clean reference point. Later runs can each change one factor against it: switching to an image-only model (config_004/006), adding images with concat fusion (config_019/003), moving to multiprofile with avgpool (config_012), or swapping the RNA encoder (config_026 PCA, config_005 scGPT). 3. Why it is the best next use of the budget: starting with a complex multimodal, multiprofile model would mix many design choices, so its result could not be attributed to any one of them. A simple baseline sets the bar that more complex models must beat, rather than assuming they will win, and makes every later comparison easier to interpret.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run, the RNA-only, single-profile scVI baseline (config_017: accuracy 0.507, F1 0.455). We know nothing yet about whether the image modality adds value, which is the most basic design question in this space. 2. Test: config_019 keeps everything from config_017 the same (single-profile, scVI RNA encoder) and only adds image features (ViT-L) with simple concat fusion. This isolates the effect of going multimodal against the existing baseline. 3. Why now: Whether to include images affects most of the remaining configurations, so resolving it early guides the rest of the search. Using concat rather than weighted fusion, and staying single-profile, avoids changing several choices at once. ViT-L is a reasonable first image encoder to try; a gain or loss here tells us whether image or encoder comparisons are worth further budget.

1) Evidence so far: adding ImageNet ViT-L image features to scVI RNA (config_019, multimodal concat) gave 0.579 accuracy and 0.563 F1. RNA-only scVI (config_017) gave 0.507 and 0.455. We cannot yet tell whether this gain comes from combining the two modalities or simply from the image features being more informative. 2) Image-only ViT-L single-profile completes the modality comparison with the same encoders. If it matches or beats 0.579, RNA adds little and later experiments should focus on image representations. If it scores clearly lower, fusing the two modalities adds real value, and it is worth tuning RNA encoders and fusion. 3) This is a single-factor control that resolves the most basic open design question, which is what drives performance. Answering it first should guide whether we spend the limited budget on multiprofile, aggregation, or fusion variants.

1. Evidence: Image-only with imagenet_vit_l is clearly the strongest result so far (acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Adding scvi_n200 RNA through concat fusion lowered performance to 0.579, and RNA-only reached just 0.507. This points to image features as the main source of signal, though each result is a single run. Profile setting is still completely untested. 2. This experiment keeps the best configuration (image_only, imagenet_vit_l) and changes only one factor: singleprofile becomes multiprofile, using the simpler avgpool aggregation. That isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps. Avgpool keeps the change minimal before trying transformer aggregation. 3. It exploits the strongest direction while answering a key open design question. If multiprofile helps, it suggests a promising axis for later multimodal and aggregation comparisons. If it does not, we avoid spending budget on the many multiprofile configurations. Testing fusion variants such as weighted fusion (config_014) is a reasonable alternative, but it is less urgent because multimodal currently trails image-only by a wide margin.

Evidence: image-only single-profile ViT-L is clearly the best so far (0.725 acc / 0.685 F1). Adding scVI RNA by concat lowered performance (0.579), and RNA-only was weak (0.507). Moving the same image model to multiprofile with avgpool collapsed performance to 0.421. The open question is whether that collapse comes from the multiprofile setting itself or from the avgpool aggregation, which may wash out informative profile-level signal. This experiment keeps the image-only ViT-L setup and multiprofile setting fixed and changes only the aggregation to a transformer, so it isolates that one factor. If it recovers or beats 0.725, multiprofile with learned aggregation becomes a strong direction to exploit, including for later multimodal runs. If it stays low, the evidence that multiprofile is harmful here gets much stronger, and the remaining budget can go to single-profile choices such as fusion type and encoders. Either result resolves a major design uncertainty, which makes it a better use of one run than another fusion or encoder variant.

Evidence: image-only single-profile ViT-L (config_006) is clearly best (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Adding scVI RNA by concatenation (config_019) dropped performance to 0.579. RNA-only scored 0.507. Multiprofile aggregation hurt image-only models with both avgpool and transformer. The key open question is whether RNA is inherently uninformative or whether naive concatenation lets the weaker modality degrade the image signal. Test: config_014 changes only the fusion method (concat to weighted) relative to config_019, keeping single-profile, scVI and ViT-L fixed. This isolates the effect of fusion. Why now: if weighted fusion recovers or beats image-only, the multimodal branch becomes worth exploiting. If it does not, that is fairly strong evidence to deprioritize multimodal configurations, which make up most of the remaining space. Either way, it prunes the search efficiently under a limited budget.

Evidence: the single-profile image-only ViT-L model (config_006) is clearly the best so far, at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Adding scVI RNA lowered performance with both concat (0.579) and weighted fusion (0.518). RNA-only with scVI is weak (0.507). Multiprofile image-only models with ViT-L degraded sharply under avgpool (0.421) and transformer aggregation (0.260). So the image branch in single-profile mode carries most of the signal, but the image encoder has been tested only with ViT-L. Test: config_004 is the same setup with ResNet50 as the image encoder. This changes one variable and isolates the effect of image representation within the best-performing setting. Why now: under a limited budget, this both exploits the strongest direction and resolves a key open design choice. If ResNet50 matches or beats ViT-L, it changes which backbone should anchor later fusion and multiprofile tests. If it is worse, it confirms ViT-L as the image encoder for future experiments.

Evidence: single-profile image-only ViT-L is clearly best (0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Adding scVI RNA lowered performance with both concat (0.579) and weighted fusion (0.518), and scVI RNA-only is weak (0.507). Multiprofile aggregation also hurt the image model badly. The main open question is whether RNA is inherently weak here or whether scVI is just a poor RNA representation, since scVI is the only RNA encoder tested so far. This experiment tests scGPT RNA-only in the same single-profile setting as config_017, so the RNA encoder is the only change. If scGPT is much stronger, retrying multimodal fusion with scGPT is justified. If it is also weak, the budget should go to image-centric configurations rather than more multimodal combinations. Under a limited budget, this one clean comparison tells us whether the large multimodal part of the search space is worth exploring.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is single-profile image-only ViT-L (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Adding scVI RNA lowered performance under both concat (0.579) and weighted fusion (0.518). Multiprofile aggregation hurt image models badly, with avgpool at 0.421 and transformer at 0.260. RNA-only models are weak and close together (scVI 0.507, scGPT 0.519), and pca_n2000, the third RNA representation, has not been tested. One possible reason fusion hurts is that the RNA features are too weak or noisy. 2. Test: Single-profile RNA-only with pca_n2000 completes the RNA encoder comparison. It changes only the representation, against two existing baselines. 3. Why now: This is a cheap, cleanly isolated experiment that answers whether any RNA representation is strong enough for multimodal fusion to be worth more budget. If PCA clearly beats the others, PCA+ViT-L concat (config_002) becomes the logical next test. If it does not, the evidence favours concentrating on image-only single-profile models instead of spending runs on multimodal or multiprofile variants.

Evidence: The two best unimodal encoders are clearly identified. PCA_n2000 is the strongest RNA encoder (0.721 vs about 0.51 for scVI and scGPT), and ViT-L is the strongest image encoder (0.725 vs 0.471 for ResNet50). Multiprofile aggregation has done poorly for image-only models (avgpool 0.421, transformer 0.260 vs 0.725 singleprofile). Multimodal fusion so far has only used the weak scVI RNA encoder. With scVI, concat (0.579) beat weighted (0.518), but both fell below image-only ViT-L, so that gap may come from the weak RNA input rather than from fusion itself. Test: config_002 pairs the best RNA encoder (PCA) with the best image encoder (ViT-L), keeping singleprofile and the better-observed concat fusion. Compared with config_019, it changes only the RNA encoder. This shows whether fusion adds value once both modalities are strong. Why now: It is a controlled extension of the strongest evidence. It has the highest chance of beating the roughly 0.72 baseline. It also settles the key question of whether multimodality helps here, before spending budget on the multiprofile settings, which look unpromising.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which choices matter: modality, profile setting, encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_034 is the simplest available model. It uses RNA only, a single profile and a PCA encoder, with no aggregation or fusion to confound the result. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that every more complex choice must beat to justify itself. 3. Why it is the best next step: Without a simple baseline, later gains from multiprofile aggregation, image features, fusion or learned encoders (scVI, scGPT) cannot be read clearly. Each can then be tested by changing one factor at a time from this anchor, such as config_045 or config_009 for multiprofile and config_030 or config_021 for the encoder. Starting here avoids assuming that more complex models are better.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run, an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.520, F1 0.479). We have no evidence yet on whether profile setting, encoder, aggregation, modality or fusion matter. 2. Test: config_045 keeps the RNA-only setting and the PCA encoder, and changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether combining multiple profiles helps, without confounding it with a learned transformer aggregator, a different encoder or image data. 3. Why now: Profile setting is a major design axis that affects a large share of the remaining configurations. A clean one-variable comparison against the existing baseline gives the most interpretable information per experiment. It also sets up later tests of aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) and of adding images.

1. Evidence: Only RNA-only PCA models have been tested. Moving from singleprofile to multiprofile avgpool gave a small gain in accuracy (0.520 to 0.530) and a larger gain in F1 (0.479 to 0.515). We have no evidence about how much signal the image modality carries on its own. 2. This experiment tests an image-only model (ViT-L) using the same multiprofile avgpool setup as the current best, config_045. It differs from that run only in modality, so it gives a direct comparison of RNA versus image information. 3. Knowing the image-only baseline is needed to read any later multimodal result. Without it, a weak multimodal model could not be traced to uninformative images or to poor fusion. This single run reduces the largest open uncertainty, whether images are worth including, before spending budget on the many multimodal fusion and encoder combinations.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (0.530 acc, 0.515 F1). It slightly beats single-profile PCA (0.520), with a clearer gain in F1. Image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool is much weaker (0.411). The biggest open question is whether adding images helps or hurts an RNA model that is already better on its own. 2. Test: config_024 combines the two tested unimodal branches: PCA RNA plus ViT-L image, multiprofile, avgpool. It adds simple concat fusion. Everything else matches config_045 and config_047, so the comparison isolates the effect of adding the image modality. 3. Why now: Whether multimodal fusion pays off determines how the remaining budget should be spent. If it gains, later runs can tune fusion type and aggregation. If it does not, the budget should shift to RNA encoders such as scVI and scGPT. Concat is the simplest baseline fusion, so it gives a clean reference before trying weighted fusion.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is the multimodal, multiprofile model with PCA RNA, ViT-L image features, avgpool and concat (config_024). It reached 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1, well above RNA-only (0.530) and image-only (0.411). Adding multiple profiles helped RNA-only only slightly (0.520 to 0.530), though F1 rose more (0.479 to 0.515). Every multiprofile run has used avgpool, so we do not know whether a learned transformer aggregation adds value. 2. Test: config_048 keeps everything from config_024 except the aggregation, which switches from avgpool to transformer. Any difference can then be attributed to aggregation alone, at the current best setting. 3. Why now: This both exploits the strongest direction and resolves an untested design axis that applies to every multiprofile configuration. The answer will tell us whether later multiprofile runs should use transformer or avgpool before we spend budget on secondary choices like fusion type or RNA and image encoders.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the stronger single modality (about 0.52-0.53 versus 0.41 for image-only). Fusing both modalities with multiprofile input helps (0.635). Switching aggregation from avgpool to transformer gave a large further gain to 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1 in config_048. So far, every multimodal run has used pca_n2000 for RNA, so we do not yet know whether the RNA representation matters, even though RNA carries most of the signal. 2) What this tests: config_015 keeps the best setup fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the RNA encoder alone. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: representation of the dominant modality is likely to have a bigger effect than fusion type or image backbone. Testing it on top of the current best both exploits the strong transformer result and reduces uncertainty about a major untested design axis. The result will also tell us whether scGPT, or scVI by extension, is worth exploring further.

1. Evidence so far: multimodal multiprofile models clearly beat unimodal ones (about 0.64–0.72 versus 0.41–0.53). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 7 points with PCA (0.706 vs 0.635). scGPT edged out PCA under the transformer setup (0.725 vs 0.706), which is a modest gain. Fusion has never been varied: every multimodal run used concat, so it is the largest untested uncertainty among the core design choices. 2. config_002 keeps the current best setup (scGPT, ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of fusion strategy. 3. It is a single-factor test on the strongest configuration. It answers whether fusion matters, and it may also improve on the best result. Testing ResNet50 or scVI next would be less useful, because fusion has no evidence at all, while encoders already have some.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multimodal models clearly beat single-modality ones (0.64–0.72 vs at most 0.53). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 7 points with PCA (0.706 vs 0.635). Concat beat weighted fusion by a wide margin with scGPT (0.725 vs 0.586). scGPT was slightly better than PCA (0.725 vs 0.706; F1 0.685 vs 0.667), a small gap that should not be overread. The image encoder has never been varied: every image-based run used imagenet_vit_l. 2. What this tests: config_004 keeps the best configuration (config_015: scGPT, multiprofile, transformer, concat) and swaps only the image encoder from ViT-L to ResNet50. This isolates the image representation choice in the strongest context. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: the image encoder is the largest untested design axis. Fixing everything else makes the comparison clean. It also has a realistic chance of beating the current best, so it balances exploration with exploitation. Testing scVI (config_039) is the natural follow-up.

Evidence: the strongest region is multimodal, multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. Within it, scGPT (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1) slightly beats PCA (0.706 acc, 0.667 F1). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool for PCA (0.706 vs 0.635). Concat clearly beat weighted fusion (0.725 vs 0.586). Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 collapsed performance (0.260). The one untested design choice in this best setting is the third RNA encoder, scVI. This experiment changes only the RNA encoder (scVI_n200) and keeps everything else fixed. It will show whether the RNA representation matters beyond the small scGPT-vs-PCA gap, and whether a compact probabilistic embedding can match or beat scGPT. It is the best use of the next run because it exploits the strongest evidence while isolating a single factor. It could also produce a new best result, and it completes the RNA-encoder comparison in the most relevant setting before spending budget on secondary questions such as single- vs multi-profile ablations.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_015 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion), at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Within the multiprofile multimodal setting, transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.706 vs 0.635), concat beat weighted fusion, and ViT-L beat ResNet50 by a wide margin. The profile setting is still the major untested axis for multimodal models. It has only been compared for RNA-only PCA, where multiprofile gave a small gain (0.530 vs 0.520). 2) Test: config_026 keeps the best encoders and fusion (scGPT + ViT-L, concat) and switches only to singleprofile, which by design removes aggregation. This shows whether the gains come from multiprofile context with learned aggregation, or whether a simpler single-profile multimodal model performs about as well. 3) Value: Profile setting is a core design choice that may change how later experiments are prioritized. A single controlled comparison against the current best settles it more directly than further fine-tuning of encoders or fusion that are already well supported.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence about which design choices matter. 2) config_027 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool, concat) is a mid-complexity anchor. It uses the simpler choices for aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat), paired with commonly strong encoders. 3) Most other design choices are one change away from it among the available configurations: weighted fusion (config_041), transformer aggregation (config_005), ResNet50 image encoder (config_008), scVI or scGPT RNA encoder (config_003, config_046), image-only (config_009) and RNA-only (config_042). That makes it the most efficient first experiment, because every later single-factor comparison against it can isolate the effect of one design choice.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: Only one result exists so far. The multimodal, multiprofile model (PCA-2000 RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.514 accuracy and 0.498 F1. With a single data point, we cannot tell whether the RNA branch adds anything beyond the image features. 2) What this tests: config_009 keeps everything the same (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool) but removes the RNA modality. This is a clean one-factor ablation of multimodality. If image-only matches or beats 0.514, the next experiments should focus on image representation and aggregation. If it falls clearly below, RNA fusion is contributing and is worth refining (RNA encoder, fusion type). 3) Why now: Model setting (unimodal vs multimodal) is the most basic design choice and determines how to spend the rest of the budget. Settling it early with a controlled comparison is more informative than tuning secondary choices like fusion or aggregation around an unvalidated multimodal baseline.

1. Evidence: the multimodal model (PCA-2000 RNA, ViT-L images, avgpool, concat; config_027) reached 0.5136 accuracy. The image-only counterpart (config_009) reached 0.5121. Fusion therefore adds almost no accuracy, though F1 rose about 0.02. This leaves it unclear whether RNA carries useful signal on its own or only slightly rebalances class predictions. 2. What it tests: config_042 is RNA-only with the same PCA-2000 encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. It completes a controlled three-way modality comparison where only the modality changes. It will show whether RNA alone is weak, comparable to images or complementary. 3. Why now: modality contribution is the most important open design question. Settling it first tells us where to spend the remaining budget, whether on RNA encoders and fusion strategies or on image-centric and aggregation variants, before tuning secondary choices like transformer aggregation or weighted fusion.

1. Evidence: RNA-only (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) clearly leads at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Multimodal concat (0.514) is about the same as image-only (0.512). This suggests concatenation lets the weaker image features swamp the stronger RNA signal. The key open question is whether that failure comes from the fusion method or from adding images at all. 2. config_041 changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, and keeps PCA, ViT-L, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This directly isolates the fusion effect. If weighted fusion matches or beats RNA-only, multimodal is still worth exploring with better fusion. If it stays near 0.51, we can confidently focus the remaining budget on RNA-only encoders and aggregation. 3. This one-factor comparison settles whether the large multimodal branch of the search space is worth exploring, which makes it the most informative next experiment under a limited budget.

1. Evidence: The RNA-only model (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool; config_042) is clearly the best so far at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Adding images hurt. Concat fusion fell to about 0.514, weighted fusion fell to 0.260, and image-only (ViT-L) reached only 0.512. RNA therefore appears to carry most of the signal. However, we have tested only one RNA encoder (PCA), so how much the RNA representation matters is still unknown. 2. Test: config_034 swaps PCA for scVI and keeps everything else fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder on the strongest branch found so far. 3. Why now: Encoder choice is a high-impact design decision, and this test changes only one variable. It exploits the promising RNA-only direction while reducing uncertainty that also bears on later multimodal and aggregation experiments. A better encoder would raise the performance ceiling. A worse one would make PCA the backbone to carry forward into tests of aggregation (e.g., config_031) and profile setting (e.g., config_036).

Evidence: the RNA-only PCA (pca_n2000) multiprofile avgpool model is clearly the best so far (acc 0.639, F1 0.620). It beats scVI RNA-only (0.573), image-only (0.512) and both multimodal fusions (concat 0.514, weighted 0.260). Every completed run used avgpool, so we have no evidence on whether transformer aggregation over profiles helps, even though aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration. Test: config_031 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer, which isolates the effect of aggregation. Why now: it exploits the strongest direction while settling an important open design choice. If the transformer helps, it is a likely new best and points to which multiprofile variants to try next. If it hurts, avgpool is supported as the default and the budget can move to profile setting or RNA encoder comparisons.

1. Evidence: RNA-only models with pca_n2000 are clearly the strongest so far (0.639 with avgpool, 0.653 with transformer). Image-only (0.512) and multimodal fusion (concat 0.514, weighted 0.260) both underperform, so adding images has not helped yet. PCA beat scVI. All six experiments used the multiprofile setting, so the profile-setting choice is completely untested. 2. This run tests RNA-only pca_n2000 in the singleprofile setting. It changes only the profile setting relative to the best RNA-only runs. Aggregation becomes None, which follows necessarily from using a single profile. The result will show whether multiprofile aggregation gives a real gain over single-profile inputs. 3. Profile setting is a major design axis with no evidence yet. Testing it on the strongest and simplest model family gives a clean comparison and answers it with one experiment. A different RNA encoder could instead be tested with scgpt, but that would add less information about an unexplored design dimension.

1) Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile models are clearly strongest. PCA with transformer aggregation reached 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1, and PCA with avgpool reached 0.639. Multiprofile beat singleprofile (0.591), and PCA beat scVI under avgpool (0.639 vs 0.573). Multimodal fusion with ViT underperformed RNA-only, with concat at 0.514 and weighted fusion collapsing to 0.260. The RNA encoder appears to be the main lever, yet scGPT, the third encoder option, is completely untested. 2) Test: scGPT RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation differs from the current best (config_031) only in the RNA encoder. It therefore directly tells us whether a foundation-model embedding beats PCA within the best known setup. 3) Why now: this is a single-variable change on the strongest configuration. It covers the largest remaining uncertainty in the most influential design choice, and it has a real chance of becoming the new best. It is more useful than more multimodal variants, which current evidence suggests are hurt by the image modality.

Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA multiprofile with transformer aggregation (0.653 accuracy). Swapping avgpool for transformer improved RNA-only PCA modestly (0.639 to 0.653, with F1 also up). Multimodal PCA+ViT with avgpool and concat (0.514) did worse than RNA-only and about matched image-only, so image features may be diluting the RNA signal under simple pooling. Weighted fusion failed badly (0.260), so concat is the better fusion to keep. The open question is whether multimodal fusion is inherently unhelpful here or only limited by avgpool aggregation. Config_005 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) relative to config_027, cleanly isolating that effect within the multimodal setting. If it approaches or beats 0.653, it is a strong exploitation candidate. If it stays near 0.51, that is solid evidence to stop investing in ViT-based multimodal models and focus on RNA-only refinements.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only pca_n2000 is the strongest direction so far. With transformer aggregation it reaches 0.653 accuracy, versus 0.639 with avgpool. The best multimodal run (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) is lower at 0.599. Image-only vit_l is weak at 0.512, which suggests the image features may be adding noise rather than signal. However, every image run so far has used imagenet_vit_l, so the image-encoder choice is completely unexplored. 2. What this tests: it keeps the best multimodal setup fixed (multiprofile, pca_n2000, transformer, concat) and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50. This isolates whether a different image representation can close or reverse the gap between multimodal and RNA-only. 3. Why it is the best next run: the open question with the most impact is whether multimodality can help at all, and this is a clean one-variable test of it. If resnet50 helps, multimodal becomes a viable path to beat 0.653. If it does not, we gain stronger evidence to focus the remaining budget on refining RNA-only models.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we have no baseline and no information about which design choices (modality, representation, profile setting, aggregation, fusion) matter. 2. What this tests: config_050 is the simplest setup, an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (n=2000) encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference point for validation accuracy and F1 on this task. Every later configuration can be compared against it to see whether added complexity actually helps. Those additions include learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), the image modality, multiprofile aggregation and fusion. 3. Why now: under a limited budget, starting from a well-defined minimal baseline is the most informative first step. It avoids the confounding that comes from starting with a complex multimodal or multiprofile model, where several design choices change at once. It also lets the next experiments vary one factor at a time from a known anchor, such as the RNA encoder (config_001 or config_034) or the modality (an image-only single-profile model).

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile, PCA baseline (config_050) reached 0.519 accuracy and 0.480 F1. Nothing is yet known about how profile setting, encoder, modality or fusion affect performance. 2) Test: config_016 keeps the modality (RNA only) and encoder (PCA) the same and switches to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation, average pooling. That makes it a near single-factor test of whether pooling information across multiple profiles helps. 3) Why now: profile setting divides much of the remaining search space, since most configurations are multiprofile. A clean answer here will narrow later choices more than changing several factors at once, such as jumping to a multimodal configuration. Average pooling is the minimal aggregation, so the profile effect is less confounded by aggregation complexity than it would be with a transformer.

1. Evidence: The two completed runs are both RNA-only with PCA. Single-profile (0.519 acc, 0.480 F1) and multiprofile with avgpool (0.518 acc, 0.484 F1) perform almost identically. So profile setting with simple averaging appears to matter little for RNA. The biggest open question is whether imaging adds anything, and we have no image evidence yet. 2. Test: config_012 keeps the single-profile PCA RNA baseline from config_050 and adds ViT-L image features through simple concat fusion. Any difference in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed mainly to adding the image modality. 3. Why now: Modality is likely the highest-impact design choice. Comparing against an existing baseline gives an interpretable, low-confound answer. That answer will guide whether later budget goes to multimodal fusion and aggregation choices or back to RNA-encoder and aggregation exploration such as scVI, scGPT or transformer aggregation.

Evidence: the multimodal PCA+ViT-L concat model (0.527 acc, 0.510 F1) slightly beats RNA-only PCA (0.519 acc, 0.480 F1). The F1 gain (+0.03) is larger than the accuracy gain. Multiprofile avgpool gave no clear benefit for RNA-only PCA. The key open question is where the multimodal gain comes from, because the image modality has never been tested on its own. Test: an image-only ViT-L singleprofile run completes a clean modality ablation, alongside the single-profile RNA-only and multimodal runs. It shows whether ViT-L image features alone match or exceed the fused model, which would make the RNA contribution marginal, or are clearly weaker, which would support fusion as complementary. Why now: this one-variable comparison sets how to spend the remaining budget. It tells us whether to prioritize image-centric configurations, RNA encoder variants (scVI, scGPT), or fusion and aggregation choices, rather than guessing from a single multimodal result.

1. Evidence: RNA carries nearly all of the signal so far. RNA-only PCA reached about 0.519 accuracy, ViT image-only only about 0.208, and multimodal concat about 0.527. Multimodal concat gave a small accuracy gain but a clearer F1 gain (0.510 vs 0.480). Multiprofile avgpool did not help RNA-only (0.518 vs 0.519). Every run so far used the PCA RNA encoder, so the RNA representation is the biggest untested choice. 2. Test: config_001 keeps the config_050 baseline (RNA-only, single profile) and changes only the encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. This isolates whether a learned latent representation beats PCA. 3. Why now: RNA dominates performance, so its encoder probably has more leverage than fusion type, aggregation or image encoder. The result tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal and multiprofile experiments, which makes the rest of the budget more efficient. scGPT (config_034) is the natural follow-up comparison.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the largest effect seen so far. pca_n2000 (0.519 accuracy) clearly beat scvi_n200 (0.427). Image-only ViT-L is weak (0.208). Multimodal concat gave only a small accuracy gain (0.527 vs 0.519), though F1 rose more (0.510 vs 0.480). Multiprofile avgpool made no real difference for RNA-only. The third RNA representation, scGPT, has never been tested, and RNA carries most of the predictive signal. 2) Test: Running scGPT RNA-only singleprofile is a one-variable comparison against config_050 (PCA) and config_001 (scVI). It shows whether a foundation-model embedding beats or trails PCA, without fusion or aggregation confounds. 3) Why now: A 9-point gap between encoders is far larger than the effects of fusion or profile setting seen so far. Settling the best RNA encoder therefore tells us which encoder all later multimodal and multiprofile runs should build on. That is worth more than fine-tuning fusion around an encoder that may not be the best.

Evidence: scGPT is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.586 acc / 0.574 F1, versus 0.519 for PCA and 0.427 for scVI). Image-only ViT-L is weak (0.208), but adding ViT-L to PCA with concat fusion gave a small gain (0.519 to 0.527 acc) and a clearer F1 gain (0.480 to 0.510). Multiprofile avgpool did not change PCA RNA-only results. Open question: does the image benefit seen with PCA carry over to the much stronger scGPT representation, or do scGPT features already capture that information? Experiment: config_045 (scGPT + ViT-L, singleprofile, concat) differs from the best run, config_034, only by adding the image modality. It uses the same fusion as the PCA comparison (config_012), so it isolates the modality effect on top of the best encoder. Why now: it exploits the strongest direction while answering whether multimodality is worth pursuing. That answer determines whether the remaining budget should go to multimodal fusion and aggregation variants or to scGPT-only variants, such as multiprofile aggregation.

1. Evidence: scGPT is clearly the best RNA encoder so far (0.586 accuracy, 0.574 F1 as RNA-only single-profile). Adding ImageNet ViT-L features through concat fusion lowered it to 0.530. Image-only ViT-L is weak (0.208), so concat may be letting a noisy modality dilute a strong one. With PCA the pattern differed: concat gave a small gain (0.519 to 0.527). Fusion type has never been varied, and it is the main uncertainty about whether the large multimodal part of the space is worth exploring. 2. Test: config_005 keeps everything from config_045 (scGPT, ViT-L, single-profile) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the fusion effect. If weighted fusion matches or beats RNA-only scGPT, it suggests learned modality weighting can down-weight weak image features and makes multimodal configurations worth pursuing. If it still falls short, that strengthens the case for focusing on RNA-only scGPT variants. 3. Why now: it is a single-variable comparison against an existing result, built on the strongest encoder. Its outcome guides many remaining candidates, since most untested configurations are multimodal weighted or concat variants. The profile-setting question is lower priority because multiprofile avgpool gave no gain with PCA (0.518 vs 0.519).

1) Evidence: scGPT RNA-only singleprofile (config_034) is clearly the best result so far (acc 0.586, F1 0.574). Adding ImageNet ViT-L images lowered scGPT to 0.530 with concat and to 0.260 with weighted fusion. Image-only performance is weak (0.208). For PCA, multiprofile with avgpool performed about the same as singleprofile (0.518 vs 0.519). Transformer aggregation has never been tested, and multiprofile has never been tested with the strongest encoder. 2) Test: this experiment keeps the best encoder and the RNA-only setting fixed. It changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the untested transformer aggregation. A direct comparison with config_034 will show whether learned aggregation across profiles adds value beyond the singleprofile result. 3) Why now: it exploits the strongest direction (scGPT, RNA-only) while exploring the least-understood design choice. The image and weighted-fusion directions already look unpromising, and the PCA result suggests avgpool gives little benefit, so a learned aggregator is the more informative multiprofile test under the budget. If it gains, avgpool (config_027) can serve as a follow-up control.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_009 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scGPT, transformer aggregation) at 0.629 accuracy and 0.599 F1. It beats single-profile scGPT (config_034) at 0.586. However, the gain could come from using multiple profiles or from the transformer aggregator, and we cannot yet tell which. For PCA, multiprofile with avgpool (config_016) did not improve over single-profile (config_050), which hints that aggregation may matter. Separately, adding ImageNet ViT images hurt scGPT performance in single-profile runs, so multimodal extensions carry more risk for now. 2. Test: config_027 keeps everything from config_009 except aggregation, which becomes avgpool. This isolates the effect of transformer versus mean pooling for the strongest encoder. If it lands near 0.629, the multiprofile setting itself drives the gain. If it lands near 0.586, the transformer aggregator is the key ingredient. 3. Why now: this is a one-factor comparison anchored on the current best configuration. It resolves a central design question cheaply and will guide whether later multiprofile and multimodal experiments should use transformer aggregation.

1. No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence on modality, profile setting, encoder, aggregation or fusion, and no baseline. 2. config_039 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) is a mid-complexity anchor. It has a one-factor neighbor for every design choice among the untested configurations: config_033 (transformer aggregation), config_007 (concat fusion), config_028 (ViT-L image encoder), config_002 and config_020 (scGPT and PCA RNA encoders), and config_006 (single-profile). Unimodal neighbors such as config_015 and config_004 can later test whether multimodality helps at all. 3. Under a limited budget, starting from a well-connected central point lets each later experiment isolate a single design effect. Avgpool and weighted fusion are simple, robust defaults, so this first run should give a reasonable performance reference without assuming the most complex model is best.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile model (scVI-n200 RNA + ResNet50 image, avgpool, weighted fusion) reached 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. With no baseline, we cannot tell whether that score comes from combining modalities or mostly from one of them. 2. Test: config_015 keeps everything the same (multiprofile, scVI-n200, avgpool) but removes the image branch and fusion. It is a clean single-factor ablation of the image modality's contribution. 3. Why now: whether multimodality helps at all decides how the rest of the limited budget should be spent. If RNA-only matches or beats the multimodal model, encoder and fusion tuning should focus on RNA. If it falls clearly below, image and fusion variations are worth exploring. This is more informative now than tweaking a secondary choice such as fusion type or aggregation.

Evidence: with scVI-200, multiprofile and avgpool held fixed, RNA-only (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1) beat multimodal ResNet50 weighted fusion (0.586 acc, 0.574 F1). Adding the image branch therefore appears to hurt, but one pair of runs cannot say why. Question: the matched image-only run (ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) completes a controlled RNA / image / fusion triad. It will show whether ResNet50 image features carry useful signal and fusion is the problem, or whether the image representation itself is weak. Why now: the answer decides where the remaining budget goes. A weak image branch points to focusing on RNA encoders and aggregation, or trying the ViT-L image encoder. A reasonable image branch points to testing other fusion choices such as concat.

1. Evidence: Within the multiprofile, avgpool, scvi_n200/resnet50 setting, RNA-only leads (0.650 acc / 0.628 F1). Adding resnet50 image features with weighted fusion lowered performance (0.586), and image-only was weakest (0.485). So RNA is the strongest modality so far, but we do not yet know whether the multiprofile setting itself helps. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the RNA-only scvi_n200 model and switches only the profile setting to singleprofile, where aggregation does not apply. This isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation on the best branch found so far. 3. Why now: Profile setting is a key design choice that affects how every later configuration should be read, and it has not been tested at all. A single-variable comparison on the strongest baseline resolves it cheaply. If singleprofile matches or beats multiprofile, later experiments can focus on encoders and fusion rather than aggregation. If it is worse, that supports exploring multiprofile aggregation further (for example, transformer in config_009).

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). Multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile for RNA-only scVI (0.650 vs 0.435). Image-only was weak (0.485), and adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion lowered performance (0.586). Aggregation has never been varied; every multiprofile run used avgpool. 2. Test: config_009 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while keeping the best configuration otherwise identical. This isolates whether learned attention over profiles beats simple pooling. 3. Why now: Aggregation matters only in the multiprofile setting, which looks like the most influential choice so far. The result will guide all later multiprofile experiments, unimodal or multimodal. It is a low-risk exploitation of the strongest setup that also resolves a key open design question, so it is a better use of budget than further multimodal runs that change several things at once.

1) Evidence so far: the best result is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1). Within RNA-only, multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile (0.435), and avgpool clearly beat transformer (0.525). Image-only did poorly (0.485), and multimodal weighted fusion with ResNet50 (0.586) did not beat RNA alone. The RNA encoder is the largest untested design choice, because only scVI has been tried, even though RNA is the strongest modality. 2) This run keeps the best setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps scVI for scGPT. That isolates the effect of the RNA representation, and the F1 score will help judge any small difference. 3) Under a limited budget, this is a controlled, one-factor comparison around the current best. It could directly improve on the best result. Either way, it tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal and fusion experiments.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1). Within that same setup, scGPT dropped sharply (0.471). Adding ResNet50 images through weighted fusion also hurt (0.586), image-only was weak (0.485), and transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool (0.525). The RNA representation therefore looks like a decisive factor, but pca_n2000 has not been tested at all. 2) This run keeps everything fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only the encoder to pca_n2000. That completes a clean three-way encoder comparison and shows whether a simple high-dimensional linear representation can match or beat scVI. 3) RNA is the strongest modality and the encoder choice carries through every multimodal configuration, so resolving it with one isolated change reduces the most uncertainty per experiment. It could also directly produce a new best model.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile avgpool models are strongest so far (pca_n2000 0.653, scvi_n200 0.650). Image-only resnet50 is weak (0.485). Adding resnet50 images to scVI with weighted fusion lowered accuracy to 0.586, so the image branch currently looks like a liability. All image results so far use resnet50, so we cannot tell whether imaging itself adds little or resnet50 is just a poor image representation. This experiment swaps only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l, keeping image-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. That makes it a clean comparison with config_004. If ViT-L clearly beats 0.485, the many untested ViT-based multimodal configurations become worth exploring. If it does not, we can deprioritize multimodal and image-heavy configurations and spend the remaining budget refining the RNA-only branch. This one run resolves a key uncertainty that affects most of the remaining search space.

1. Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile avgpool models are the strongest so far (pca_n2000 0.653, scvi_n200 0.650 accuracy). The one multimodal run (config_039: scvi_n200 + resnet50, weighted fusion) scored lower at 0.586, and image-only models are weak (0.41-0.48). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation and multiprofile beat singleprofile, each in a single comparison. Fusion is the only design choice not yet varied: we cannot tell whether the multimodal shortfall comes from the image modality or from the weighted fusion. 2. What this tests: config_007 matches config_039 except for fusion (concat instead of weighted). This isolates the fusion effect. If concat recovers or exceeds RNA-only performance, fusion was the bottleneck. If not, image features are likely adding noise and the search should focus on RNA-only variants. 3. Why now: this single-variable comparison resolves the main open question about whether multimodal models are worth exploring further. That answer decides how much of the remaining budget should go to the many untested multimodal configurations.

1) Evidence: The two best runs are RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool models with PCA (0.653 acc / 0.628 F1) and scVI (0.650 / 0.628), which are effectively tied. Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat singleprofile (0.435) and transformer aggregation (0.525) for scVI. Image-only models are weaker (ResNet50 0.485, ViT-L 0.411). Adding images with weighted fusion (scVI+ResNet50, config_039) lowered accuracy to 0.586 versus scVI RNA-only at 0.650. Concat fusion failed badly (0.208). The open question is whether that weighted-fusion penalty is general or specific to one run or encoder pairing. 2) Test: config_020 changes only the RNA encoder from config_039 (scVI to PCA), keeping multiprofile, avgpool, ResNet50 and weighted fusion. Comparing it with config_024 (PCA RNA-only) and config_039 shows whether weighted fusion with images can match or beat the strongest unimodal baseline, and whether the fusion gap holds across RNA encoders. 3) Why now: this is a one-variable change that both exploits the best-known RNA setting and addresses the most important unresolved design choice, whether multimodal fusion adds value. The alternatives look weaker. PCA with transformer aggregation or singleprofile would repeat choices that already hurt scVI, and the concat or ViT-L variants have poor priors.

1) No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters, and no reference point for judging gains. 2) config_014 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest configuration available. It sets a baseline that later runs can each change one factor from: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), modality (image-only, multimodal), and profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer). 3) Under a limited budget, a cheap and interpretable anchor lets every later experiment act as a clean one-factor comparison. It also guards against assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better without evidence.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: We have one result, RNA-only single-profile PCA (acc 0.332, F1 0.315). We know nothing yet about the image modality, so we cannot tell whether multimodal fusion is likely to help or which modality carries more signal. 2. What this tests: config_019 is the matched image-only single-profile baseline with ResNet50. It keeps the profile setting the same and uses no aggregation or fusion, so the comparison isolates the effect of modality. 3. Why now: Establishing the image-only baseline is the most foundational open question. Fusion, aggregation and encoder choices are only interpretable once both unimodal baselines are known, and this experiment changes a single dimension rather than several at once.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only ResNet50 (single-profile) reached 0.471 accuracy and 0.442 F1. RNA-only PCA (single-profile) reached 0.332 accuracy and 0.315 F1. So image features look stronger, but we do not know whether RNA adds information that complements the image. 2. What this tests: config_030 fuses the same two encoders (PCA plus ResNet50) by simple concatenation, still in the single-profile setting. Only one thing changes from the image-only baseline: RNA is added. The result shows whether multimodality helps, does nothing, or hurts, with no confounding from a new encoder, aggregation or profile setting. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Whether to go multimodal is the most important branching decision, since most remaining configurations are multimodal. Answering it cleanly now will guide how the rest of the budget is spent. Encoder swaps and multi-profile aggregation can be explored afterward against a clear baseline. Concat is chosen over weighted fusion as the simpler, more interpretable first test of fusion.

1) Evidence so far: all three experiments use singleprofile with pca_n2000 and resnet50. Image-only (0.471 accuracy) clearly beat RNA-only (0.332). Concat fusion improved further to 0.518 accuracy and 0.484 F1. The profile setting is completely untested, and it is a major design axis that may matter more than encoder or fusion details. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_030: pca_n2000 + resnet50 + concat) and switches only to multiprofile. It uses avgpool, the simplest aggregation, which is needed whenever there are multiple profiles. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be credited mainly to using multiple profiles rather than to new encoders or fusion. 3) This is the best use of the budget because it builds directly on the strongest result while removing the largest remaining uncertainty. The answer tells us whether later experiments should concentrate on the multiprofile part of the space, including comparing transformer with avgpool aggregation, or stay with singleprofile.

1) Evidence so far: image-only (ResNet50, 0.471) clearly beats RNA-only (PCA, 0.332), so the image branch carries most of the signal. Single-profile concat fusion (0.518) gives a modest gain over image-only. Multiprofile avgpool (0.520) is essentially tied with single-profile, and its F1 is slightly lower, so profile setting looks like a weak lever for now. The image encoder has never been varied, even though it is probably the most influential remaining choice. 2) This run swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L, compared against config_030 (single-profile, PCA, concat). That isolates the effect of the image representation. 3) Given the limited budget, testing the encoder of the dominant modality inside the current best simple setup is the most informative next step. 1) Evidence and uncertainty: the image encoder is the dominant lever so far. Why now: this single-factor change answers the main unresolved design question, whether multimodal fusion is worth it. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have one result so far, an RNA-only single-profile scVI baseline at 0.519 accuracy and 0.480 F1. 1. Evidence: config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) is clearly best at 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1.
