It exploits the strongest direction found so far and answers an open design question with a single-variable change. The result will also guide which aggregation to carry into the remaining multimodal and RNA experiments.

1. Evidence: Image-only ViT-L is clearly the strongest branch so far (0.591 with avgpool, 0.599 with transformer). Transformer's edge over avgpool is too small to trust. Multimodal concat with scGPT (0.535) and RNA-only scGPT (0.520) both trail image-only. Every run so far used the multiprofile setting, so the effect of profile setting is completely unknown. 2. This run tests the single-profile version of image-only ViT-L, keeping the modality and encoder of the best model. Comparing it with config_002 and config_030 isolates whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps or whether single-profile inputs do as well. 3. With a limited budget, this answers the biggest open design question within the most promising direction. It also tells us whether later runs, including multimodal ones, should focus on multiprofile or single-profile settings.

Evidence: image-only multiprofile with imagenet_vit_l is the strongest direction so far, at 0.599 accuracy with transformer aggregation and 0.591 with avgpool. That aggregation gap is small, so I don't treat it as conclusive. Multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile for image-only (0.591 vs 0.525). Concat fusion with scGPT RNA (0.535) and RNA-only (0.520) both underperformed image-only. The largest untested axis in the dominant modality is the image encoder, since resnet50 has never been tried. Test: config_016 differs from the best run (config_030) only in swapping imagenet_vit_l for resnet50. This isolates whether the image representation drives performance. Why now: image features appear to carry most of the signal, so knowing which encoder is better guides nearly all remaining configurations, including multimodal ones. That makes this single-variable comparison a high-value use of the next experiment, ahead of retuning fusion or RNA encoders.

Evidence: the best result so far is image-only, multiprofile, ResNet50 with transformer aggregation (config_016, acc 0.653, F1 0.628). ResNet50 beat ViT-L by about 0.054 under the same transformer setup. Transformer aggregation was only slightly better than avgpool for ViT-L (0.599 vs 0.591). The one multimodal run (config_022, scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) scored 0.535, below its image-only counterpart (0.591), and scGPT RNA-only was weak (0.520). The main open question is whether adding RNA ever helps, or whether concat fusion simply dilutes a strong image signal. That rests on a single comparison made with the weaker image setup. Test: config_015 keeps the best image setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer) and adds scGPT RNA with concat fusion. Against config_016, the only difference is adding the RNA branch. Against the earlier config_002 vs config_022 pair, it shows whether the multimodal penalty holds with a stronger backbone and aggregator. Why now: this answers the highest-value design question, multimodal vs image-only, at the current best operating point, so the result is useful either way. If RNA still hurts, the budget can go to image-side refinements (e.g., config_046 or single-profile ResNet). If it helps or matches, follow-ups on fusion type (config_049) and RNA encoder (config_050 or config_018) become well motivated.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is image-only ResNet50 with transformer aggregation (0.653 accuracy). Adding scGPT RNA with concat fusion (config_015) slightly lowered accuracy to 0.635. scGPT RNA-only was weak (0.520). Every RNA result so far uses scGPT, so it is unclear whether RNA adds little in general or whether scGPT is simply a poor RNA representation here. 2. Test: config_018 changes only the RNA encoder from scGPT to scVI. Everything else matches config_015 (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion). This isolates the effect of RNA representation in the strongest region found so far. 3. Why now: this is the largest open uncertainty, and the answer decides where the remaining budget should go. If scVI closes or reverses the gap to image-only, RNA and multimodal fusion are worth exploring further. If it still trails, focus can shift to image-only refinements or fusion type with more confidence.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: ResNet50 with multiprofile transformer aggregation is the strongest setting so far. Image-only config_016 reached 0.653 accuracy, and multimodal scVI concat (config_018) reached 0.650, statistically indistinguishable. Concat fusion has not shown clear value from adding RNA, and weighted fusion has never been tested, so fusion is the largest open design choice. 2) What this tests: config_043 differs from config_018 only in fusion (weighted instead of concat). It therefore isolates whether learned modality weighting lets RNA add complementary signal, or at least avoid diluting the strong image features. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: it explores an untested dimension while staying in the highest-performing region, so it has good odds of a new best result. Either outcome is informative about whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing over image-only models.

1. Evidence: The strongest setup so far is multiprofile + resnet50 + transformer aggregation. Image-only (config_016) reached 0.653 accuracy. Adding scVI RNA with concat fusion (config_018) gave 0.650, and adding scGPT RNA (config_015) gave 0.635. So the RNA encoder appears to matter, but no RNA representation has yet beaten image-only. The pca_n2000 RNA encoder has not been tested at all. Weighted fusion collapsed in its one trial (0.427), so concat is the safer fusion choice. 2. Test: This run keeps profile setting, image encoder, aggregation and fusion fixed at the best-known values and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. Compared with config_015 and config_018, it completes a clean three-way comparison of RNA encoders. Compared with config_016, it shows whether any RNA representation adds value over image-only. 3. Why now: It explores the one untested encoder while staying inside the best-performing region. It changes a single factor, so the result is directly interpretable. It also has a reasonable chance of beating the current best.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which design choices matter: modality, profile setting, RNA or image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. 2) config_051 (RNA-only, single-profile, scVI with 200 dimensions, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest reasonable configuration. It sets a reference accuracy and F1. Later runs that change one factor can then be compared against it: adding images (e.g., config_045 or config_050), switching to multiprofile (config_042 for avgpool, config_002 for transformer), or changing the RNA encoder (config_038 for PCA, config_015 for scGPT). 3) Under a limited budget, starting with a cheap, low-complexity anchor avoids assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models are better. It makes every later experiment interpretable as a one-factor change, rather than starting from a complex configuration where any result would be hard to attribute.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile scVI baseline (config_051) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1, so nothing is yet known about which design choices matter. 2) What this tests: config_042 keeps the modality (RNA-only) and encoder (scvi_n200) fixed. It changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This gives a clean, one-factor test of whether aggregating multiple profiles helps, without confounding it with a more complex transformer aggregator, image features or fusion choices. 3) Why now: profile setting is a key structural decision that most remaining configurations depend on. Resolving it early with a minimal change gives the most interpretable information per experiment, and it tells us whether multiprofile variants such as transformer aggregation and multimodal fusion are worth pursuing next.

1. Evidence: With the scVI RNA-only setup, single-profile reached 0.713 accuracy (F1 0.695). Multi-profile with avgpool fell to 0.520 (F1 0.498). That large drop could mean multi-profile input is harmful in itself, or that avgpool is a poor way to combine profiles. Two runs cannot tell these apart. 2. Test: config_002 keeps model setting (RNA-only), profile setting (multi-profile) and encoder (scVI) fixed and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. If accuracy recovers toward or above 0.71, avgpool was the bottleneck and multi-profile designs remain viable. If it stays near 0.52, the multi-profile setting itself is likely the problem. 3. Value: Most of the remaining search space uses multi-profile input with either avgpool or transformer aggregation, including many multimodal configurations. This one-variable comparison therefore tells us whether that large region deserves budget before we spend runs on encoder or image modality choices.

1. Evidence: all three runs so far are RNA-only with scvi_n200. The single-profile model is best (acc 0.713, F1 0.695). Multiprofile underperformed it with both aggregators: transformer reached 0.635 and avgpool only 0.520. So single-profile looks like the stronger setting for now. The biggest open question is whether imaging adds anything, since no image-based configuration has been tested. 2. Test: config_050 keeps the best configuration unchanged (single-profile, scvi_n200, no aggregation) and adds only a ResNet50 image encoder with simple concat fusion. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to adding image features, not to profile setting or RNA encoder. 3. Why now: whether to fuse modalities shapes the rest of the search, since most untested configurations are multimodal. A one-variable comparison against the current best answers this efficiently. If fusion helps, it points toward exploiting multimodal single-profile variants. If it does not, the budget can shift to RNA encoder comparisons such as scgpt or pca_n2000 in the single-profile setting.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is single-profile RNA-only with scVI (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). Multiprofile aggregation lowered accuracy (transformer 0.635, avgpool 0.520). Concat fusion with ResNet50 images in the single-profile setting failed badly (0.227). Every run so far has used scVI, so we do not know whether the RNA representation itself is a major factor. 2) Test: Keep the strongest setting (RNA-only, single-profile) and change only the RNA encoder to PCA with 2000 components. This isolates the effect of representation without the confounds of image features or fusion. 3) Why now: It exploits the best-performing direction while answering a key open design question with a clean one-factor comparison. A PCA result above or below scVI tells us whether to keep scVI or switch encoders in all later experiments, including any multimodal ones. That is a better use of the budget than more multimodal runs, which so far show strong negative evidence.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is the simplest model, RNA-only single-profile scVI (0.713 acc, 0.695 F1). The RNA encoder clearly matters: PCA in the same setting scored only 0.421. Multiprofile underperformed in both tests, though the transformer (0.635) beat avgpool (0.520). Multimodal concat with ResNet50 collapsed to 0.227. The scGPT encoder is still completely untested. 2) Test: Running scGPT in the best-performing setting changes only the RNA encoder. It shows whether a foundation-model representation beats scVI, which is the most influential design choice observed so far. 3) Why now: It extends the strongest configuration while removing the largest remaining uncertainty about RNA representation. It is a clean single-variable comparison. Its result will also tell us which RNA encoder to carry into later multiprofile and fusion experiments. Questions about weighted fusion or image-only signal are better answered once the best RNA backbone is known.

1) Evidence: scVI single-profile RNA-only is the clear leader (0.713 acc / 0.695 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_050) collapsed performance to 0.227. That collapse could come from concat fusion letting weak image features swamp the RNA signal, or from ResNet50 features being harmful in general. This is a single result, so it should not yet be read as proof that multimodal models fail. 2) This experiment keeps everything from config_050 fixed (scVI, ResNet50, single-profile) and changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above the RNA-only baseline, fusion was the problem and multimodal models remain viable. If it stays poor, the image features themselves are the likely problem, and image-only or ViT-L tests become the logical next step. 3) It is the best next use of the budget because it is a clean one-variable comparison of a design choice that affects every multimodal configuration, which is most of the remaining options. It also has a reasonable chance of matching or beating the current best, since a learned weighting can down-weight an uninformative modality.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only single-profile scVI (0.713 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 image features lowered accuracy, to 0.619 with weighted fusion and 0.227 with concat. The image modality has never been tested alone, so it is unclear whether the images carry little signal or whether the fusion methods are the problem. 2. Test: Image-only, single-profile, ResNet50 isolates how much signal ResNet50 image features carry, using the same image encoder and profile setting as the multimodal runs. 3. Why now: A weak result would suggest images are mostly noise, so the search should focus on RNA, especially aggregation (transformer beat avgpool). A moderate or strong result would support further work on fusion and image encoders (ViT-L). Either way, this one run settles a key uncertainty that affects a large share of the remaining configurations.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only single-profile scVI (0.713 acc, 0.695 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion lowered accuracy to 0.619, and concat fusion collapsed to 0.227. Multiprofile aggregation also hurt RNA, though transformer (0.635) beat avgpool (0.520). Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.535. The ImageNet ViT-L image encoder has never been tested, yet it appears in about half of the remaining configurations, so the quality of the image representation is the largest unresolved design choice. 2) What this tests: config_046 is image-only, single-profile ViT-L, which differs from config_040 (image-only ResNet50) only in the image encoder. It therefore isolates whether ViT-L gives a stronger image representation, without fusion or aggregation effects mixed in. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: If ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50, multimodal weighted fusion with scVI and ViT-L (config_011) becomes a credible way to surpass the RNA-only baseline. If it does not, most ViT-L multimodal configurations can be deprioritized, which saves budget either way.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is the simplest model, scVI RNA-only single-profile (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). For multiprofile RNA, transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.635 vs 0.520). For multimodal single-profile, weighted fusion far outperformed concat (0.619 vs 0.227), though it still trailed RNA-only. The two image encoders performed about the same on their own (0.535 vs 0.532). 2. Test: This configuration pairs the best-performing choices, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion, in a multiprofile multimodal model with scVI and ResNet50. Compared with config_045, it adds multiprofile with transformer aggregation. Compared with config_002, it adds the image modality through weighted fusion. It is still a two-variable change against each anchor, so if it underperforms we cannot tell which addition caused it. 3. Why now: Whether multiprofile multimodal modeling can beat the simple RNA-only baseline is the main open question about the whole multimodal and multiprofile direction. Answering it is more valuable than swapping image encoders, which showed no difference on their own. It also stays within the configuration space the evidence favors.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so there is no information on whether modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters, or what accuracy level is achievable. 2. Test: config_033 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest configuration available. It sets a reference baseline. Each later comparison can then change one factor against it: image-only (config_006/014), multimodal fusion (config_001/018), multiprofile aggregation (config_026/048) or learned RNA encoders (config_031/036). 3. Why now: without an anchor, gains from more complex multimodal or multiprofile models cannot be read reliably. A cheap, interpretable baseline makes every later experiment more informative under the limited budget, and it guards against assuming complexity helps.

1. Evidence: only one result exists. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_033) reached 0.328 accuracy and 0.288 F1. We do not yet know whether imaging adds any signal, and modality is likely the most consequential design choice. 2. Test: config_001 keeps the same RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and profile setting (singleprofile), and adds an image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) through simple concat fusion. Comparing it with config_033 isolates the effect of adding the image modality. 3. Why now: this one-factor change answers the highest-level question first, whether multimodal input helps at all. That answer decides whether later budget should go to fusion, image-encoder and multiprofile variants, or to RNA-side improvements. Concat is the simplest fusion, so it is a clean first test, and later image-only runs can help attribute any gain.

Evidence: the multimodal PCA+ViT-L concat model (0.586 acc, 0.574 F1) far outperforms RNA-only PCA (0.328 acc). This shows the image modality adds a lot, but we cannot yet tell whether fusion helps or whether images alone explain the gain. What it tests: image-only ViT-L in the single-profile setting differs from config_001 only in removing RNA. It therefore isolates RNA's contribution to the multimodal result. Why now: whether multimodal fusion beats a strong unimodal image baseline is the most important unresolved design question. Its answer decides whether later budget should go to fusion, aggregation and RNA encoder choices, or mainly to image-based and multiprofile extensions.

Evidence: in single-profile mode, multimodal PCA plus ViT-L with concat fusion (config_001, acc 0.586, F1 0.574) clearly beats image-only ViT-L (0.519) and RNA-only PCA (0.328). Fusing the two modalities helps, and image features carry most of the signal. Profile setting is still completely untested, and it may be one of the most consequential design choices. Test: config_043 keeps the best configuration's encoders (PCA, ViT-L) and fusion (concat) and switches only to multiprofile. It uses avgpool, the simplest aggregation, so the comparison against config_001 mainly isolates whether multiprofile input helps. Why now: this exploits the strongest known configuration while answering a high-impact open question with a near-single-variable change. If multiprofile helps, later runs can compare transformer against avgpool aggregation (config_039) and weighted against concat fusion. If it does not, the budget can go to single-profile refinements such as encoder or fusion swaps.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is single-profile multimodal (PCA + ViT-L, concat) at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. Moving to multiprofile with avgpool, with every other choice the same, dropped performance to 0.471 / 0.442. That drop could come from the multiprofile setting itself or from avgpool, which may wash out useful information across profiles. This is the largest unresolved effect in the history. 2. Test: config_039 keeps PCA, ViT-L and concat fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. If the transformer recovers or beats 0.586, multiprofile is still worth pursuing with learned aggregation. If it stays low, multiprofile can be deprioritized and the budget focused on single-profile encoder and fusion choices. 3. Why now: This one-variable comparison settles whether a whole branch of the search space (multiprofile configurations) deserves further budget. That is more valuable than a small exploit tweak such as a fusion or encoder swap in the single-profile setting.

1. Evidence: the single-profile multimodal model (PCA + ViT-L, concat; config_001) is best so far at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. It beats image-only (0.519) and RNA-only PCA (0.328). Both multiprofile variants scored lower (avgpool 0.471, transformer 0.331), so single-profile is the promising direction for now. The RNA branch looks weak with PCA, and the RNA encoder is still untested. 2. Test: config_032 keeps everything in config_001 the same (single-profile, ViT-L, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI. This isolates whether a learned RNA representation adds more to fusion than PCA does. 3. Why now: it exploits the best context while testing a major untested design choice with a single change. A gain would point to RNA representation as a key lever. No gain would suggest the RNA contribution is limited regardless of encoder.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is the single-profile multimodal model with PCA RNA and ViT-L image features using concat fusion (config_001, acc 0.586, F1 0.574). It beats image-only (0.519) and RNA-only (0.328), so fusing both modalities seems to help. Multiprofile aggregation did worse in both forms tried (avgpool 0.471, transformer 0.332). Swapping PCA for scVI also lowered accuracy (0.523). Fusion strategy is the one major design choice not yet tested: every multimodal run used concat. 2) This experiment keeps config_001 fixed and changes only concat to weighted fusion. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the fusion method. 3) Under a limited budget, this one-factor change exploits the strongest configuration while closing the largest untested gap. Weighted fusion may also cope better with the weaker RNA modality. Either outcome tells us whether fusion should be explored further, for example in the multiprofile settings.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_028 (single-profile, PCA RNA, ViT-L image, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Switching concat to weighted fusion gave a large gain (0.586 to 0.725). Image-only (0.519) far outperforms RNA-only (0.328), so the image representation appears to be the main source of signal. However, every experiment so far has used ViT-L, so the effect of the image encoder is still unknown. Test: config_008 changes only the image encoder (ViT-L to ResNet50) and keeps the rest of the best configuration fixed. This isolates the image-encoder effect within the strongest setup. Why now: because image features drive most of the performance, the choice of image encoder is the most important design decision left untested. This one-variable comparison either confirms ViT-L as the backbone to keep exploiting or reveals a better option. It is more informative than retrying multiprofile variants, which have performed poorly, or testing RNA-encoder swaps, which matter less given RNA's weak standalone signal.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_028 (single-profile, PCA + ViT-L, weighted fusion; accuracy 0.725, F1 0.685). Switching fusion from concat (config_001, 0.586) to weighted was the largest gain observed. Among RNA encoders, scVI underperformed PCA under concat (0.523 vs 0.586), and scGPT has never been tested, so RNA representation is the biggest remaining unknown. Multiprofile runs have only been tried with concat and did poorly (0.471 avgpool, 0.332 transformer). 2) Test: config_044 keeps the best setup and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation improves on PCA when paired with the strongest fusion. 3) Why now: it explores a completely untested design choice while staying anchored to the best-known setup, so it could yield a new best. Even if it does not, it shows whether RNA representation matters under weighted fusion. Testing whether weighted fusion rescues multiprofile (config_004) is a sensible follow-up, but current evidence on multiprofile is negative, so resolving the unexplored encoder is the better use of this experiment.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_028 (PCA + ViT-L, single profile, weighted fusion; 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Weighted fusion clearly beat concat with the same encoders (0.725 vs 0.586). PCA has beaten scVI and scGPT so far. Multiprofile has only been tried with concat fusion. There it underperformed single profile (avgpool 0.471, transformer 0.332 vs 0.586). That leaves open whether multiprofile fails on its own or only fails with weak concat fusion. 2) Test: config_004 keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion and moves to the multiprofile setting with avgpool aggregation. Avgpool was the better multiprofile aggregation in earlier runs. This isolates the profile-setting question under the strongest known fusion. 3) Why now: Profile setting is an important design choice whose current evidence is confounded with the weaker fusion method. The encoder evidence already consistently favors PCA, so another encoder run would teach less. This run is a logical extension of the best configuration and also directly reduces a key uncertainty.

1) No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about representation, profile setting, aggregation or fusion. 2) config_002 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) is a central anchor. Each design factor can be isolated from it with one change: fusion (config_027), aggregation (config_021), RNA encoder (config_011, config_017), image encoder (config_030), profile setting (config_024) and modality (config_001 image-only, config_009 RNA-only). 3) Starting here gives a reference point for controlled one-factor comparisons and a plausible estimate of how well a full-featured model performs. Later unimodal and single-profile runs can then test whether the added complexity is actually needed, without assuming it is.

1. Evidence: only one experiment has run. It is a multimodal, multiprofile model (scVI n200 + ImageNet ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reaching 0.512 accuracy and 0.477 F1. We have no reference point, so we don't know whether adding RNA helps. 2. Test: config_001 removes only the RNA branch and fusion. The image encoder (ViT-L), the multiprofile setting and the transformer aggregation stay the same. This isolates RNA's contribution to the multimodal result. 3. Why now: whether multimodality adds value is a top-level design question. If image-only matches or beats 0.512, later experiments can focus on image encoders and aggregation instead of spending budget on RNA encoders and fusion variants. If it underperforms, that supports continuing to explore the multimodal space. A single-factor ablation is the most informative use of the next experiment.

1. Evidence: Image-only (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) reached 0.678 accuracy. Adding scVI RNA with concat fusion, with everything else fixed, dropped accuracy to 0.512 and F1 by a similar amount. We cannot tell whether the drop comes from weak RNA signal (scVI features) or from naive concat fusion letting a noisy modality dominate. 2. Test: config_009 is the RNA-only counterpart (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer). It completes a clean three-way modality ablation under the same profile and aggregation settings. If RNA alone is far below image, the problem is RNA quality, and later experiments should look at other RNA encoders (scGPT, PCA) or weighted fusion. If RNA alone is reasonably strong, the failure points to concat fusion, and weighted fusion (config_027) becomes the logical next test. 3. Why now: it changes only one factor and resolves the main uncertainty about whether to invest in the multimodal direction at all. That makes it the most informative use of the next experiment, even though it is unlikely to be the top performer.

1) Evidence: Both unimodal transformer-multiprofile models do well (RNA scVI 0.688, image ViT-L 0.678). Combining exactly those encoders with concat fusion drops sharply to 0.512, with F1 also lower (0.477). So the multimodal failure most likely comes from how the modalities are combined, not from weak encoders. 2) Test: config_027 keeps everything from config_002 the same (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer) and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. This isolates whether concat fusion caused the drop, and whether a learned weighting can recover or exceed unimodal performance. 3) Why now: Whether fusion can make multimodal models competitive is the key unresolved question, and it shapes how roughly two-thirds of the remaining space (the multimodal configs) should be explored. A single-factor comparison against an existing baseline is the most interpretable use of one experiment. If weighted fusion still fails, that is strong evidence to favor unimodal or aggregation-focused directions.

1. Evidence: with multiprofile transformer aggregation, RNA-only (scVI, 0.688 acc) and image-only (ViT-L, 0.678 acc) clearly beat both multimodal variants (concat 0.512, weighted 0.471). The F1 scores show the same pattern. Changing the fusion method did not fix the drop, so fusion type alone does not seem to explain it. One open possibility is that transformer aggregation over fused multiprofile inputs is unstable or overfits. 2. This experiment keeps config_002 unchanged except for swapping transformer aggregation for avgpool (same scVI and ViT-L encoders, concat fusion, multiprofile). It tests directly whether aggregation is driving the multimodal degradation. 3. It is the best use of the budget because it isolates one design choice behind the largest unexplained effect so far. If avgpool recovers multimodal performance, multimodal models remain promising and worth exploiting. If it does not, the evidence would shift toward unimodal or singleprofile settings, and further fused multiprofile runs would likely be poor value.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with transformer aggregation (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1), with image-only ViT-L close behind (0.678). Multimodal models with transformer aggregation did much worse (0.512 with concat, 0.471 with weighted fusion). Switching the multimodal concat model from transformer to avgpool raised accuracy substantially (0.512 to 0.591). This suggests aggregation matters a lot, but we only know that within the multimodal setting. 2. Test: config_006 keeps the best configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI) and changes only the aggregation from transformer to avgpool. This shows whether avgpool's advantage holds generally or only in the multimodal case. It also checks whether the transformer is overfitting or poorly optimized. 3. Why now: This is a single-variable comparison on the current best setup, so the result is easy to interpret. If avgpool beats 0.688, it becomes the new best and points future runs toward avgpool everywhere. If not, we learn that the aggregation effect depends on modality, which tells us how to fix multimodal fusion. Single-profile settings remain an important untested axis for a later experiment.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: All six completed runs used the multiprofile setting. The best result so far is scVI RNA-only with transformer aggregation (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). ViT image-only with transformer is close behind (0.678). Every multimodal fusion run did worse (0.47–0.59), so multimodality has not helped yet. Aggregation choice matters a great deal: avgpool dropped RNA-only to 0.33. This raises the question of whether the multiprofile setup itself helps or hurts, and that has never been tested. 2) What this tests: config_041 keeps the strongest setup (RNA-only, scVI encoder) and switches only the profile setting to singleprofile, with no aggregation. This gives a clean, one-variable comparison of singleprofile versus multiprofile against the best configuration. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Profile setting is a major design axis with zero evidence so far. The result will guide many remaining options, because over a third of the untested configurations are singleprofile. Since aggregation looks fragile, this run will also show whether a simpler model without aggregation can match or beat the multiprofile transformer.

1) Evidence: Every multimodal run so far (multiprofile, scvi_n200 plus imagenet_vit_l) has scored below both unimodal baselines. The scores were 0.47–0.59, against 0.68 for image-only and 0.69 for RNA-only. The best result so far is single-profile RNA-only scvi_n200 at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. So it is unclear whether fusion is inherently unhelpful or whether it fails only in the multiprofile setting. 2) Test: config_024 is identical to config_002 except that the profile setting is single-profile, so it isolates the profile effect for multimodal models. Adding imagenet_vit_l images lowered accuracy, to 0.650 with weighted fusion and 0.536 with concat. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile avgpool with scVI (0.713 accuracy; scGPT is close at 0.706). Among image-only models, ResNet50 (0.639) clearly beats ViT-L (0.537). Test: this is the simplest configuration (RNA-only, single profile, PCA-2000 encoder, no aggregation or fusion). It sets a baseline for validation accuracy and F1. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal single-profile PCA + ViT-L with concat fusion (config_020, acc 0.619, F1 0.610). 1. Evidence: Single-profile multimodal (ViT-L + PCA, concat) is the best so far at 0.619 accuracy. Image-only ViT-L at 0.591 beats RNA-only PCA at 0.518. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is singleprofile multimodal PCA + ViT-L with concat fusion (config_020: acc 0.619, F1 0.610). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (multimodal, singleprofile, PCA + ViT-L, concat fusion) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Evidence: image features carry most of the signal. ViT-L image-only (0.591) far exceeds PCA RNA-only (0.518), and the best result so far, single-profile PCA+ViT-L concat (0.619), is only about 3 points above image-only. 1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so we have no baseline and no idea how hard the task is or whether any added complexity (images, multiple profiles, aggregation, fusion) is worth it. 2. What this tests: the simplest available configuration, an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000 components) RNA encoder and no aggregation or fusion. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one experiment has been run, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.494, F1 0.453). 1. Evidence: Fusion has been tested, but the profile setting has not. 1) Evidence: Single-profile multimodal fusion (PCA + ResNet50, concat; config_003) scored 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_008 (multiprofile, transformer aggregation, PCA RNA, ResNet50, concat) at 0.721 accuracy. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_008 (multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best results so far come from PCA_n2000 + ResNet50 with concat fusion. Evidence: with the same PCA-2000 RNA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, RNA-only reached 0.520 accuracy (F1 0.498). Adding ImageNet ViT-L image features with concat fusion collapsed this to 0.224 (F1 0.184). The likely causes are that concatenation lets high-dimensional, weak image features swamp the RNA signal, or that the image modality is mostly noise; from one comparison we cannot yet tell which. This experiment keeps config_008 fixed and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. That isolates fusion and tests whether a learned modality weighting can recover or beat RNA-only performance. It is the best next use of the budget because fusion is the most direct suspect for the failure and the change is a single variable. The result also guides much of the remaining space: if weighted fusion recovers performance, many multimodal weighted configurations stay promising; if it still fails, image features themselves are suspect, and image-only (config_016) or RNA-only refinements become the priority.

1. Evidence: Under multiprofile, PCA-2000 and avgpool, weighted fusion with ViT-L (config_007, acc 0.678, F1 0.646) far outperformed RNA-only (config_011, 0.520). But we have no image-only result, so we cannot tell whether the 0.678 comes from combining modalities or mostly from the ViT-L image features alone. 2. Test: config_016 (image-only, multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool) completes a clean modality ablation, with profile setting, aggregation and image encoder held fixed. If it approaches or beats 0.678, the image representation is the main driver and the search should focus on image encoders and aggregation. If it falls well below, weighted fusion adds real value, and refining fusion (e.g., transformer aggregation or other RNA encoders with weighted fusion) is justified. 3. Why now: this single experiment resolves the largest open question, where the performance comes from, before budget is spent on extensions of config_007 that assume multimodality is the cause.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_030 (pca_n2000 + resnet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.721, F1 0.681). It beat the same setup with imagenet_vit_l (config_007; 0.678).
